newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chronology of Japanese politics since 1989.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Japanese politics since 1989.

text.p: The following is a chronology of the instability in Japanese politics since 1989 when the long-ruling Liberal Democratic Party first became embroiled in a political scandal:

June 1989 - Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita of the LDP resigns over a "shares-for-favours" scandal and inept introduction of a three percent sales tax. Sosuke Uno succeeds him, but becomes embroiled in a scandal over an affair with a geisha.
July 1989 - LDP loses in Upper House polls. Uno resigns.
August 1989 - Toshiki Kaifu, dubbed "Mr Clean", is chosen as prime minister because the LDP still retains a majority in Lower House, the more powerful of parliament's two chambers.
February 1990 - Kaifu wins Lower House general elections.
November 1991 - Kaifu resigns after his party, led by strongman Ichiro Ozawa, scraps his political reforms. Former finance minister Kiichi Miyazawa takes over as premier.
January 1992 - Prosecutors arrest a Miyazawa ally for accepting bribes from a property developer.
May 1992 - Former provincial governor Morihiro Hosokawa forms anti-corruption Japan New Party.
October 1992 - Shin Kanemaru, LDP kingmaker and Ozawa's mentor, retires from politics after acknowledging he received illegal funds from a trucking firm.
December 1992 - Ozawa and Tsutomu Hata form faction in the LDP, splitting from the dominant Takeshita faction.
June 1993 - Ozawa-Hata group and second group led by Masayoshi Takemura quit the LDP, allowing parliament to pass no-confidence vote against Miyazawa, who calls snap elections.
July 1993 - The LDP loses Lower House majority in polls. Seven opposition parties agree to form coalition government and name Hosokawa as prime minister.
January 1994 - Hosokawa pushes political reform bills through parliament.

April 1994 - Hosokawa resigns after opposition LDP targets his shady links to a trucking firm. Hata becomes prime minister but the Socialists, biggest party in the bloc, walk out, leaving Hata head of a minority government.

June 1994 - Hata resigns after LDP and Socialists threaten him with no-confidence vote. Parliament elects Socialist leader Tomiichi Murayama as prime minister at head of formerly unthinkable LDP-Socialist alliance. The Sakigake Party, an LDP splinter group, joins the coalition.
July 1994 - Murayama abandons key Socialist policies including opposition to U.S.-Japan security ties.
December 1994 - Remnants of Hosokawa-Hata coalition form opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party). Party comes under effective control of Ozawa.
July 1995 - Socialists do badly in Upper House election. Murayama refuses to call Lower House elections.
August 1995 - Ryutaro Hashimoto, trade minister under Murayama, wins election as LDP president.
December 1995 - Ozawa wins opposition Shinshinto leadership election against his old ally, ex-premier Hata.
January 5, 1996 - Murayama resigns to hand power to Hashimoto and LDP. Socialists and Sakigake stay as LDP allies.
September 27, 1996 - Hashimoto dissolves the Lower House of parliament and sets October 20 as date for general elections.
September 28, 1996 - Sakigake junior member Yukio Hatoyama and Health Minister Naoto Kan launch Democratic Party of Japan. Lower House Speaker Takako Doi takes over as Socialist leader.
October 8, 1996 - Official election campaigning starts.
October 20, 1996 - Voting day.
